author: blu
body: THIS CHAPTER CANNOT RUN A MACRO AND THAT IS THE POINT. Executing one means feeding commands back through the console's dispatch, which is effectful and lives in the console; everything here is the pure half -- storing, finding, splitting, refusing. So the table and the splitter can be tested without a machine, which is the same split `DevState` made for the watch table and for the same reason.

author: blu
body: THE DANGEROUS PART OF A MACRO IS NOT STORAGE, IT IS RECURSION. A macro whose body runs a macro can reach itself, and on a machine with no collector and no stack guard that is a hang at best. The bound is NOT fuel and NOT a depth counter: the console refuses `macro.run` outright while a macro is already running. A hard refusal is checkable by reading one flag, where a depth limit has to be got right and then trusted, and nothing a debugger macro is for needs nesting.

author: blu
body: That refusal lives in the console because the flag does, but it is named here because this is where someone reading about macros will look for it, and a bound documented only at its enforcement site is a bound nobody finds.

author: blu
body: EVERY CAP REFUSES OUT LOUD. A macro silently truncated at its eighth command is worse than one rejected: the operator watches it run, sees no error, and believes the tail executed.

author: blu
body: A local trim rather than the console's. `text-trim` already exists twice in the tree and each pair raises CDX3006; adding a third definition of the name would mean the version a mention gets depends on which chapter the mention sits in. The `macro-` prefix is the cheap way not to make that worse.

author: blu
body: An EMPTY command is dropped rather than kept, so `mem ; ; perf` is two commands and a trailing `;` is not a third. An empty command handed to the dispatcher would fall through to the expression evaluator and answer an error about a name nobody typed.

author: blu
body: REDEFINING A NAME REPLACES IT rather than adding a second entry. Two entries under one name would make `macro-find` answer whichever came first, so a correction typed after a mistake would appear to do nothing; and a table of sixteen would fill with retries of the same macro.

author: blu
body: The full-table check is skipped when the name already exists, because a replacement does not grow the table. Checking it anyway would refuse an operator's fix to the sixteenth macro on the grounds that there are sixteen macros.

author: blu
body: `repeat` takes a count and a command on ONE line, which is the only two-argument command in this console. Everything else takes at most one argument because the cursor supplies the other, and a repeat has no cursor to draw on: neither half of `3 mem` is a thing the console is already pointing at.

author: blu
body: The split is at the FIRST space, so the command may contain spaces and the count may not. A missing space, a count that is not a number, and a count outside the bounds are three different mistakes and each says which it was.
